title: The Elders of the Galilee
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: At times the sages of the generation gathered there. Hyman cites Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:3 [the corresponding passage is at 2:5]: toward the end of the persecution the rabbis assembled at Usha—R’ Yehudah, R’ Nechemyah, R’ Meir, R’ Yose and others. They sent to the elders of the Galilee: “Whoever is learned should come and learn,” etc. Hyman suggests that when persecution intensified in Judea, they fled to the Galilee, where it was less severe.
And in Moed Katan, chapter 3, halakhah 1, and Nedarim, chapter 9, halakhah 1: R’ Shimon son of Rabbi did not find an opening for his vow until one of the elders of the Galilee came, etc.

notes.text: Hyman supplies Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:3; the matching Usha assembly passage is in 2:5. Its opening explicitly distinguishes learned people coming to teach from others coming to learn. Hyman’s proposed Judea-to-Galilee explanation remains his conjecture.

No new primary scalar was returned. The earlier assembly comparison is Shir HaShirim Rabbah2:5 beside supplied2:3; both are retained without a fresh whole-source claim. Supplied וילמוד can straightforwardly mean and learn, while the earlier compared teaching invitation motivates the contextual teach rendering. The running quotation now keeps learn with the reported teach comparison stated here; no uninspected pointed text is claimed. The Judea-to-Galilee flight is Hyman’s inference, not established history. All abbreviated personal titles stay R-prime except source full רבי after Shimon, retained as Rabbi without adding Yehudah. The two vow loci and unnamed elder remain separate.

Hyman’s print (vol. I, p. 405) cites Shir HaShirim Rabbah 2:3 and gives the invitation in an unpointed, abridged form. The consulted passage at 2:5 distinguishes the learned, who are to come and teach (וִילַמֵּד), from the unlearned, who are to come and learn (וְיִלְמוֹד). It continues with the rabbis’ teachings at the gathering. The consulted Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan names Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi, whereas the corresponding Nedarim text initially gives simply Rabbi Shimon. Both include a version with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar. The accounts and their variants do not establish Hyman’s reconstruction of the migration from Judea.
